fullText:
Nice work on using skills more effectively for coding agents.

(bookmark it)

In this work, researchers treat skill granularity as a runtime decision. For each task, the agent can use primitive tool calls, a macro skill, or a macro skill that falls back to primitive steps when it fails.

Fixed macro execution is efficient when the skill fits and brittle when it does not.

The controller picks the level from task structure, execution state, and earlier macro failures, and a finite-state executor handles the fallback as an explicit transition instead of an informal retry.

In a 12-task routing study, a learned router reaches 100% success where a hand-written heuristic fails. With macro-to-micro fallback, the agent recovers controlled macro failures that fixed granularity leaves unresolved.

fullText:
Can LLMs improve their own harness?

Self-improving harnesses are a hot topic.

And one interesting question is whether LLMs can generate and improve them on their own.

They find that two full rewrites of the harness raise held-out scores by only 2.80 points, and the 95% interval crosses zero.

Each frontier model writes a complete harness from a fixed coding bootstrap, plays five development games through it, and then rewrites its whole codebase twice. Every version is scored on 20 games that never influence the rewrites.

Across 27 lineages, first harnesses range from zero to near-ceiling. The revisions add very little. Gains on the development games overstate the held-out gains, and revisions that cut inference cost often lower the score.

Human-steered systems still score higher on the same games, so better designs exist. The models just do not find them reliably on their own yet.

fullText:
让Agent自己压缩、搜索、恢复历史上下文，用有限的窗口支撑十亿Token级别的累计会话

billion-context：解决长时运行时上下文爆满、Token成本高，以及压缩后丢失关键历史信息的问题

跟一次性摘要式压缩最大的区别是历史可恢复

其思路是把历史对话分层压缩，同时保留原始内容，让模型在需要时再搜索、恢复特定片段，让有限窗口通过持续压缩与恢复，来支撑十亿级Token的长会话

首先增量分层压缩：Agent可以主动选择压缩哪些历史消息，将旧上下文折叠为摘要，而不是反复压缩整段对话

按需恢复：需要追溯早期决策、代码修改或工具调用时，可以通过decompress恢复原始内容

历史搜索：通过search_context检索压缩摘要和当前可见消息，找到相关历史后再按需恢复原始内容

Prompt Cache优化：尽量保持缓存前缀稳定，减少重复计算和Token成本

举个例子，AI连续开发了一个项目数周，中途经历多次重构，第十天需要追溯第一天为什么选择某个数据库架构，可以搜索历史并恢复当时的原始讨论，而不是只能依赖一段可能遗漏细节的压缩摘要

支持面比较广，Claude Code、Codex、OpenCode、DeepSeek Harness等Coding Agent都适用

fullText:
Machine Unlearning — The Value of Imperfect Models: https://t.co/2l1rFcnOjU

Excerpt:

Statistician George Box once said that “all models are wrong, but some are useful.” With that in mind, therefore, we are reminded that when building Machine Learning models for data analytics projects, it is useful to pay attention to a little machine unlearning.

Allow your models to have a little less perfection than your data-driven instincts might prefer, and allow your science-driven intuition to permit your models to have a natural failure rate that is consistent with the natural variance in the data collection. In doing this, you pay respect to the good-old fashioned ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve in statistics.

When building, testing, and validating a suite of models, the optimal model (i.e., the optimal point in the ROC curve) is the spot where the overall accuracy of the model is essentially unchanged as we make small adjustments in the choice of model. That is to say, the change (from one model to the next) in the model’s precision (specificity) is exactly offset by the change in the model’s recall (sensitivity).

Consequently, allowing for some imperfection, where the false positive rate and the false negative rate are in proper balance (so that neither one has too great of an impact on the overall accuracy and effectiveness of the model), is good fruit from your data-intensive labors.

fullText:
new blog post by me, "The Harsh Geometry of Superintelligence--  The Selfish Supermind Attractor Generally Has a Wider Basin than the BGI Attractor"

https://t.co/HnUTwymq0Q

So ... in a series of prequel posts I have described several kinds of possible AGI mind, each with its own basic drives and each tending --  as it increases its intelligence and capability, to stay roughly the kind it starts out as..

Examples are: 

* the power-seeking maximizer of Steve Omohundro’s 2008 "Basic AI Drives" paper

* the BGI minds that my colleagues and I are trying to build, ...and half a dozen others.

Knowing what kinds of superintelligent minds are attractors under intelligence/capability increase  is only part of the puzzle, though. 

The next question is: What are the shapes of the basins of these attractors?

I.e, the zillion-dollar (actually, well, money-obsoleting…) question is: Which kind of attractor will a given early-stage AGI system fall into and how hard will it be to knock out again? 

In dynamical systems terms, this depends on how wide and how deep the basin around each one is.

So this blog post analyzes these attractor basins a bit, with an aim toward milking lessons for building AGI systems and for understanding what an AGI system should do when something strange happens to it that may potentially zoink it out of its historical attractor basin. 

The disturbing yet unsurprising punchline here is: While Omohundro’s original “Basic AI Drives” paper overstated the omnipresence of the “selfish” attractor in the space of superminds … nonetheless it DOES seem that the selfish attractor has a big, wide and deep basin that makes it especially easy for AGI systems to fall into it … if they are not designed just right….

This doesn’t mean you need some sort of extremely carefully calibrated mathematical design to avoid convergence to selfishness – but it does mean that if you don’t bother to build things like compassion and goal-continuity into your AI system’s initial goal framework, you have no reason to expect your system to converge elsewhere than to a selfish Omohundro-esque attractor as it self-modifies and its intelligence and capability increase.

Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.
